world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Retired/bookkeeping Glottolog code; entry deemed non-existent (Soriente 2005 reclassification)

sources.citation: Asih, Yuni Utami. 2017. Inventory of Kenyah Lepo Tau segmental sounds. OKARA: Jurnal Bahasa dan Sastra 11(1), 10 pp. DOI 10.19105/ojbs.v11i1.1233 (CORE 229884182).
sources.note: Segmental inventory only (18 consonants, 5 underlying vowels; vowel lengthening 'found in closed syllables'); no statement of where stress falls. Cites Lees 1965, Rufinus 1992 (Lepo' Bakung), Soriente 2003 p.77 for Lepo' Tau phonology.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2017. The Lowland Kenyah posterior implosives. Language and Linguistics 18(2): 177-200. DOI 10.1075/lali.18.2.01blu (open access).
sources.note: Appendix fn. 11 (p.198): 'Stress was invariably recorded as final in citation forms.' -- refers to Long Sela'an Kenyah (Lebu' Vu'/Lebo' Vo', LOWLAND Kenyah, an upper-Baram village; Glottolog long1406 [ttw]); Long Anap (Highland) appears only for segmental correspondences.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian Languages (rev. ed.). Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics. Sec. 4.1.3, p.186.
sources.note: Areal remark only: 'many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context'; Highland Kenyah (Lepo' Sawa, Long Anap) is cited on the same page only for syllabic nasals and syllabification (lək.koʔ vs lu.ndoʔ), not for stress.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1913. The languages of Borneo. Sarawak Museum Journal 1(4): 1-196.
sources.note: Kenyah wordlists (Lepu Tau, Lepu Anan, Lepu Sawa...) only; no Kenyah accent remark.

sources.citation: Van Genderen Stort, P. 1912. Nederlandsch-Kenja-Dajaksche woordenlijst (dialect of the Oema Bem, Apo Kayan). Verhandelingen van het Bataviaasch Genootschap 59(3).
sources.note: 'Uitspraak der klinkers' (pdf p.288): vowel letters only, no klemtoon remark (and the dialect is Uma' Bem, Kalimantan Highland Kenyah).

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: a comprehensive classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (sec. 2.11.4 Kenyah, pp. 252-256; primary data for Lepo' Tau, Lepo' Sawa, Lepo' Gah, Lepo' Laang, Badeng, Lebo' Vo', Uma' Pawe of the upper Baram).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: No stress statement for any Kenyah variety (its stress remarks concern Merap, Murik, Segai-Modang, Hliboi Bidayuh, West Kalimantan Malayic only).

sources.citation: MPI-EVA Jakarta Field Station, 'Documentation of Kenyah' project page (A. Soriente), Wayback capture 2010.
sources.note: Nothing; states 'No thorough description of any Kenyah isolect has ever been produced. The only existing documents in Kenyah are a few wordlists and a Bible translation in one isolect, Leppo Tau.'

sources.citation: Soriente, Antonia. 2008. The classification of Kenyah languages: a preliminary statement. In SEALS XIV vol. 2 (Pacific Linguistics E-5), 49-62.
sources.note: Nothing on accent; confirms that 'Upper Baram Kenyah' (Wurm & Hattori; Ethnologue 15) is a geographic label mixing dialects, and that 'Uma Tau' = Lepo' Tau = the Long Nawang dialect.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2007. Change Request 2007-265 (K. Anderbeck, with A. Soriente): retire [ubm] Kenyah, Upper Baram as non-existent (effective 2008-01-14).
sources.note: Nothing; identity only: 'Upper Baram Kenyah' is a vague geographic label (Wurm & Hattori 1981); RA: unclear to which of the two Kenyah languages it belongs.

sources.citation: Gordon, R. G. (ed.) 2005. Ethnologue, 15th ed., entry 'Kenyah, Upper Baram [ubm]' (Wayback capture 2006).
sources.note: Nothing. Gives region (upper Baram near Kalimantan border), classification 'Main Kenyah', 'Long Anap may be a dialect (Blust 1974)'.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1971. Field notebook RB2-003-A (Kaipuleohone, University of Hawai'i, Robert Blust collection, hdl 10125/33159): Long Anap (Lepo' Sawa) Kenyah section, notebook pp. 41-69 (images 020-034), speaker Dominic Lusat, 24 Aug-30 Sep 1971.
sources.note: No prose statement. Citation-form phonetic transcriptions on pp. 41-45 and 48-49 carry stress marks: the large majority are final (du'a '2', tu'jo? '7', ta'kət, mə'gut, ləma'sa, kəlu'ma, ləma'tay, bətu'?ən, kələ'put, səbu'tiŋ, məŋa'jan...), a minority penultimate ('ləma '5', 'pi?ən '9', 'pulo? '10', 'likut, 'tulay, 'tisan, 'takut, 'mata, 'laki; ta'lu ~ 'təlu '3'); stress marking stops after p. 46. First-hand data consistent with non-contrastive, predominantly final prominence in citation forms, but not a quotable rule.

sources.citation: Douglas, R. S. 1911. A comparative vocabulary of the Kayan, Kenyah and Kalabit dialects. Sarawak Museum Journal 1(1): 75-119 (Kenyah = Leppu Buau of the Baram: Leppu Tau, Leppu Jingan, Leppu Annan, Leppu Sawa).
sources.note: Pronunciation notes cover letter values only; nothing on accent.

sources.note: Nothing; 'Retired in ISO 639-3: any current use is likely either Mainstream Kenyah [xkl] or Uma' Lung [ulu]'.
